CEO Elon Musk stated this was a significant engineering challenge, as non-REE magnets (like ferrite) have much lower energy density than the neodymium-iron-boron (NdFeB) magnets commonly used. Tesla's solution combines three approaches: enhancing the synchronous reluctance path in the rotor, developing new composite ferrite materials, and using hairpin windings with improved thermal management. The result is a system-level engineering achievement rather than a single breakthrough.

This move marks a strategic pivot for Tesla. Early models used REE-free induction motors, then switched to REE-dependent permanent magnet motors for efficiency and cost during mass production. Now, with scaling and geopolitical supply chain risks in mind, Tesla is again prioritizing REE-free technology, starting with the North American-focused Cybercab. The new drive unit is designed for mass production with a sub-10-second assembly cycle, reduced factory footprint, and a reported cost reduction of around $1000 per unit.

The article analyzes the implications for Chinese companies, which currently dominate the global REE supply chain and high-performance magnet manufacturing. While this has been a key advantage, Tesla's move demonstrates that supply chain dominance does not equate to an unassailable technological moat.
